## Common `sbatch` options

We'll go through the most commonly used `sbatch` options\
(except `--account`, which you saw in the previous lecture).

<hr style="height:1pt; visibility:hidden;" />

. . .

Recall that any `sbatch` option can be:

- Passed on the command line: `sbatch --account=PAS3493 myscript.sh`
- Added at the top of the script you're submitting: `#SBATCH --account=PAS3493`

<hr style="height:1pt; visibility:hidden;" />

. . .

Also note that:

- If an option is specified in both places, the command-line option takes **precedence**.
- Many options have a long (e.g. `--account`) and a short format (e.g. `-A`).\
  For clarity, we'll stick to **long-format options** in this material.

## Time limits: introduction

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="47%"}

- The **default time limit is 1 hour** ---
  and your job will be **killed** as soon as it hits the time limit!

- You can request up to 7 days of time
  (or request access to a different queue for longer jobs).

<hr style="height:1pt; visibility:hidden;" />

::: {.callout-tip .fragment data-fragment-index="1"}
#### The time you reserve is the "**wall time**"
This is simply the amount of time that passes on the (wall) clock.
In contrast, "**core hours**" are the wall time multiplied by the number of cores.
For example, a job that runs for 2 hours on 8 cores has a wall time of 2 hours
and uses 16 core hours.
:::

:::
::: {.column width="6%"}
<div class="fragment" data-fragment-index="2" style="border-left: 1px solid #A7B1B7; height: 100%; margin: 0 auto; width: 0;"></div>
:::
::: {.column width="47%" .fragment data-fragment-index="2"}

- OSC bills projects for **the time that jobs actually used**, not what you reserved,
  and jobs stop as soon as the script has finished running.
  - Given that you're often unsure how long a job will take,
    it's common to request (substantially) **more time** than your best guesstimate.
  - While you should be aware that jobs that request more time are likely to
    **wait longer** before they start, OSC tends to have short queueing times.

:::
:::

::: footer
:::

## Time limits: how to specify

The `--time` option specifies the maximum wall time for your job.\
A number of formats can be used to specify the amount of time, including:

| Format                |  Example  |            Meaning             |
| :-------------------- | :-------: | :----------------------------: |
| minutes               |   `60`    |           60 minutes           |
| hours:minutes:seconds | `1:00:00` |           60 minutes           |
| days-hours            |  `2-12`   | two-and-a-half days (60 hours) |

: {.striped .hover}

<br>

. . .

For example, requesting 2 hours in the "minute-format" inside a shell script:

```{.bash .file filename="myscript.sh (excerpt)" code-line-numbers="false"}
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --time=120
```

## Exercise 1: Specifying time

::: callout-quiz
::: callout-note
#### 1. How would you specify 90 minutes and two-and-a-half days with `--time`?

Give two different formats for each.

<hr style="height:1pt; visibility:hidden;" />

<!-----
<details><summary> {{< fa square-check >}} &nbsp; &nbsp; _Click for the answer_</summary>

- 90 minutes: `--time=90` or `--time=1:30:00`
- Two-and-a-half days: `--time=2-12` or `--time=60:00:00`

</details>

<hr style="height:1pt; visibility:hidden;" />
------>
:::
:::

<br>

::: callout-quiz
::: callout-note
#### 2. How many core hours will OSC bill?

Your job reserved 10 hours with `--time=10:00:00` and 8 cores,
but the script finished after 2 hours.\
How many core hours will OSC bill your project for?

<hr style="height:1pt; visibility:hidden;" />

<!-----
<details><summary> {{< fa square-check >}} &nbsp; &nbsp; _Click for the answer_</summary>

16 core hours (2 hours × 8 cores):
OSC bills for the time a job actually used, not for the time you reserved.

</details>

<hr style="height:1pt; visibility:hidden;" />
------>
:::
:::

## Cores with `--cpus-per-task`

- Slurm uses the terms "core" and "CPU" interchangeably,
  and bioinformatics tools often say "thread":
  therefore **think of core, CPU, and thread as synonyms**.

- Running a program with multiple cores is very common,
  and can make it run much faster.\
  **8--12 cores** is often a sweet spot
  (more can suffer from strongly diminishing returns).

<hr style="height:1pt; visibility:hidden;" />

. . .

- Use **`--cpus-per-task`**,
  and **also tell the program** that the script runs about this number:

```{.bash .file filename="myscript.sh (excerpt)" code-line-numbers="false"}
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --cpus-per-task=8

# We tell a fictional program about the number of available cores:
trimming_program.py --cores 8 sampleA_R1.fastq.gz
```

## Memory with `--mem`

- The `--mem` option sets the maximum amount of RAM memory available to your job.
- The **default** is **4 GB per core**:
  e.g., `--cpus-per-task=4` gives you 16 GB of memory.\
  Therefore, you'll often have enough memory automatically, and may not need to specify `--mem`.
- Like with time, your job is **killed** when it hits the memory limit
  (but the error messages are less clear).

. . .

<hr style="height:1pt; visibility:hidden;" />

- The default `--mem` unit is MB (MegaBytes): append `G` for GB.
  For example, to request 20 GB:

```{.bash .file filename="myscript.sh (excerpt)" code-line-numbers="false"}
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --mem=20G
```

<br>

. . .

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
Regular Pitzer nodes have up to 178 GB of memory.
To request more, see the
[optional self-study page](../bonus/slurm.qmd#requesting-large-amounts-of-memory).
:::

## Exercise 2: Adjusting cores and memory

Which `#SBATCH` lines will you use to run a bioinformatics program in these scenarios?

::: callout-quiz
::: callout-note
#### 1. `--cores 12`, needs 60 GB of memory

A) `--cpus-per-task=12`
B) `--cpus-per-task=12` and `--mem=60G`
C) `--cpus-per-task=12` and `--mem=60`

<hr style="height:1pt; visibility:hidden;" />

<!-----
<details><summary> {{< fa square-check >}} &nbsp; &nbsp; _Click for the answer_</summary>

**B**: the default memory for 12 cores is only 48 GB (option A),
and option C would request only 60 MB.

Alternatively, you could ask for 15 cores
(which gives you 60 GB of memory),
and tell the program to use 12 or all 15 of them.

</details>

<hr style="height:1pt; visibility:hidden;" />
------>
:::
:::

<hr style="height:1pt; visibility:hidden;" />

::: callout-quiz
::: callout-note
#### 2. `--threads 8`, needs 25 GB of memory

A) `--cpus-per-task=8`
B) `--cpus-per-task=8` and `--mem=25G`

<hr style="height:1pt; visibility:hidden;" />

<!-----
<details><summary> {{< fa square-check >}} &nbsp; &nbsp; _Click for the answer_</summary>

**A**: 8 cores give you 8 × 4 = 32 GB of memory, so you don't need `--mem`.
Option B would also work,
but there is no point in "downgrading" the amount of memory.

</details>

<hr style="height:1pt; visibility:hidden;" />
------>
:::
:::

## Slurm log file names with `--output`

- By default, the Slurm log file is created in the dir from which you submitted the script,
  and is called `slurm-<job-id>.out`, e.g. `slurm-12431942.out`.

. . .

- It can be useful to include the purpose of the script in the Slurm log file name,
  typically by including the name of the program that the script runs.

- You'll want to **keep the job ID** in the file name too,
  so log files from different runs don't overwrite each other.
  Since you won't know the job ID in advance, use **`%j`**, which represents the job ID:

```{.bash .file filename="myscript.sh (excerpt)" code-line-numbers="false"}
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --output=slurm-fastqc-%j.out
```

<hr style="height:1pt; visibility:hidden;" />

::: {.callout-warning .fragment}
#### I prefer not to include a dir in `--output`
For one, that dir must already exist when you submit the job:
otherwise, the job fails right away, **without even producing a log file**.
See the [optional self-study page](../bonus/slurm.qmd#copying-the-slurm-log-file-to-the-output-dir)
for additional considerations.
:::

## Notification emails with `--mail-type`

Slurm can email you when a job begins, completes successfully, or fails ---
at the address linked to your OSC account. I recommend the following:

<br>

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="47%"}

### [Shorter jobs (up to a few hours)]{style="display:block; text-align:center;"}

Only get emails if they **fail**:

```{.bash .file filename="myscript.sh (excerpt)" code-line-numbers="false"}
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --mail-type=FAIL
```

Especially when you submit many jobs at a time,
you may otherwise overlook failures for some jobs.

:::
::: {.column width="6%"}
<div class="fragment" data-fragment-index="1" style="border-left: 1px solid #A7B1B7; height: 100%; margin: 0 auto; width: 0;"></div>
:::
::: {.column width="47%" .fragment data-fragment-index="1"}

### [Longer jobs (> a few hours)]{style="display:block; text-align:center;"}

Get emails when they **fail or finish**:

```{.bash .file filename="myscript.sh (excerpt)" code-line-numbers="false"}
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --mail-type=END,FAIL
```

You don't want to have to keep checking in on jobs that run for many hours.
(But for shorter jobs, you may get inundated with emails
and then quickly start ignoring them altogether.)

:::
:::

## Summary of `sbatch` options

::: {.smaller-table}

| Resource/use                                     | long option example                            | short option |    default     |
| ------------------------------------------------ | ---------------------------------------------- | ------------ | :------------: |
| Project to be billed                             | `--account=PAS3493`                            | `-A`         |     *N/A*      |
| Time limit                                       | `--time=4:00:00`                               | `-t`         |    1:00:00     |
| Nr of cores                                      | `--cpus-per-task=1`                            | `-c`         |       1        |
| Memory limit per node                            | `--mem=20G`                                    | &mdash;           |  4G per core   |
| Log output file                                  | `--output=slurm-fastqc-%j.out`                 | `-o`         | `slurm-%j.out` |
| Get email when job fails<br>/ ends or fails      | `--mail-type=FAIL` <br> `--mail-type=END,FAIL` | &mdash;       |  *(none)*               |

: {.striped .hover tbl-colwidths="[25,40,15,20]"}

:::

<br>

. . .

for later reference.
:::
